Extinction of the Great White Shark

By: Liz Fish | Delivery

Proposal


Show:

Summary:
The Great White Shark population along the South African coastline is facing extinction- there are insufficient breeding pairs to create genetic diversity, there is also only one species of Great Whites off our coastline. A six year study by Dr Sara Andreotti from the University of Stellenbosch along with “shark man” Michael Rutzen a shark behaviourist has found that there are between 353 to 522 Great Whites left and only 333 individuals can contribute offspring to the next population and can carry on the 14 million year lineage.

Further information:
Dr Andreotti’s first study which Carte Blanche covered revealed that a sharks dorsal fin is like it’s thumb print. Andreotti has built a data base of photographs and has crossed checked it with the DNA samples collected from every shark they have photographed. Spending 4 years collecting samples and photographs, often at sea for two months at a time, with over 5000 siting’s, the data revealed an alarming situation. They were seeing the same sharks. They were migrating between Gansbaai, False Bay and Port Elizabeth but it was the same population, and there are only between 353 and 522. This study has confirmed what conservationists have feared, but now they have concrete evidence.
Great Whites are supposedly a protected species yet The Natal Sharks Board is killing between 11 - 60 great whites annually, a staggering 10-15% of the population. South Africa also issues permits to legally long line sharks and so it is little wonder that the species is in such a dire state. Other reasons for the decline include baiting, poaching for the honour of owning a shark jaw; habitat encroachment and depletion of their food sources.
The loss of an apex animal impacts the food chain, fewer sharks means more seals which in turn means fish stocks decline, coupled with over fishing food security for local fishermen is impacted

Press Release:


Great Whites
South Africa’s Great White shark population has plummeted to alarming numbers. A recent study revealed that there may be less than 530 Great Whites along our coastline, confirming fears that the species may be rapidly facing extinction. Carte Blanche asks: Are we doing enough to protect Great Whites?


Script:


Script: Great Whites, the feared and loved masters of the oceans with a lineage dating back 14 million years, could be facing extinction according to Marine biologist Dr Sara Andreotti from Stellenbosch University’s Evolutionary Genomics Group. She says there are only between 353 and 522 left in South African waters, and they face a double jeopardy
Sara: It has been estimated that you need a minimum of 500 breeders to maintain evolutionary potential in a population. I didn’t find 300 adults in the population anymore
Script: That means there is just one generation of Great Whites left in the South African waters. Sara research found 52 % fewer than in previous studies. Along with 7 others she recently published an academic paper that’s had the Shark community buzzing.
Sara “My professor just came back from an overseas conference where top notches in the field were explaining how to use genetic to estimate population numbers and they are already using our paper as an example of a work well done”
Script: Finding and counting these mysterious creatures is no easy task, Sara teamed up with Mike Rutzen, a well know character in Gansbaai, the white shark capital of the world. Mike free dives with sharks and operates a cage diving business. He’s noticed a steady decline in both size and number of Great Whites since 2005
Mike “I am very worried about my future due to the numbers she brought back to us it is alarming”
Script: For the last 6 years he’s been finding her sharks and funding the research
LINK: When scientists want to discover the size of an animal population on land, they can use fancy cameras, helicopter surveys. But when the study subjects are deep-diving, migratory sharks, it gets a bit more complicated
Sara “The key of counting great whites is identifying them. If you see the same shark 20 times you mustn’t count 20 sharks so what we have to do is finger print every individual so we recognise them when they come back and we did so by taking very high quality photos of their dorsal fin they are unique for each shark “
Script: Mike’s job is to lure them in with chum and keep them coming back until she gets the shot
Derek- Did you get it
Sara “No I am getting it but it is not completely out
Script: It’s easier said than done
Script: In 4 years she took over 5000 images but to her surprise she was seeing the same sharks over and over, they struggled to find more than 400 individual sharks. But photo identification is limited as it only captures the trap happy sharks that come to the boats
Link: Counting great whites is even more tricky because they move around sometimes over great distances so the sharks off the South Africa coast are not always home and they don’t always frequent every hotspot
Script: It was clear she needed another method of verifying her findings and started to collect flesh samples, matching every photograph with their DNA.
Sara “In the labatory I could run the genetic and then double check that my photo identification was correct and it was always correct
Script: Most of the samples were collected in Gansbaai, so to ensure her findings were representative of the whole area, they set sail from Port Nolloth to Algoa Bay spending months at sea
Sara “Based on previous studies that have been done its been estimated that you need a minimum of 100 genetic samples are required to have a confident of the population size based on the DNA and we collected 233 sharks which is more than double the required amount on-top of it is has been said that a minimum of 10 markers are required to do this kind of estimate and we received 14. So based on the comments through the peer review process I am very confident that our result as are as accurate as we could make it”
Script: The study not only showed that the Great white’s numbers were dramatically down but 89% were from the same lineage. The paper sparked a major debate, her fellow scientists in the White Shark Research Group strongly disagreed with the findings. Alison Towner also working with Photo IDs in Gansbaai, over roughly the same period, estimated the population to be between 800-1000 for Gansbaai alone.
Alison “There is no disregarding the fact that they have put in a good effort in terms of getting the study together the problem lies in the fact that the general consensus is not that the scientists agree with them, and we want the best scientific numbers to come out at the end of the day.
Derek “Some scientist argue you have taken too few samples over too short a period of time from too small an area
Sara “Well if 5 years is short period of time, 5000 photos is not a good sample size, and 303 genetic samples is not a good sample size in their opinion, they must do better that is all I can say
Script: These controversial results have spurred the rest of the Group to drop what they are doing and collaborate on a scientific response, arguing science with science. But Sara maintains her work is not comparable with previous studies as hers is the first comprehensive genetic study basing her findings on the largest genetic sample globally available
Mike “Once the debate is over maybe we have no sharks left because we in the field see a rapid decline and Sara numbers are alarming
Script: But the shark scientists all agree on one thing- wiping out an apex predator impacts the balance of the whole ecosystem. For example the Seal population has increased, which is diminishing the fish stocks which in turn threatens the survival of other species like the African Penguin
Alison “Great White sharks face a multitude of threats in SA waters particularly a real concern of mine is the inshore long liners and illegal fisheries that are taking unquantified amounts of many different species of sharks not just the Great Whites and then of course it crosses international borders where there aren’t protective measures in place such as Mozambique.
Script: Great Whites have been protected in South Africa for the last 25 years but despite this they are being caught on baited hooks and in gill nets along the KZN coastline. We are literally fishing out any shark that comes into the protected bathing areas
Link “The KZN Sharks board is mandated to protect bathers along the coast line but every year they catch around 550 sharks, 26 of those are Great Whites, only 20% of them survive
Script: Head of research Geremy Cliff says the only consolation is that every shark is used for scientific research
Derek “Has this study put pressure on the sharks board to find an alternative?
Geremy “It has but we have recognised that pressure. There is growing environmental awareness about the marine environment , traditionally when the nets went in the thinking was the only good shark is a dead shark but people’s attitudes have changed and we have made a huge effort to try and reduce catches in the nets by removing the nets during the sardine run, removing the nets that are not popular as bathing areas by replacing nets with baited lines so we have brought our annual catch down from just over 1400 sharks to just over 500 sharks,
Script: Gcobani Popose Director of Coastal Conservation Strategies for the Department of Environmental Affairs says the study needs to be seen in the context of all the other studies, but he is confident they are doing enough to protect the Great Whites.
Gcobani” Sharks in South Africa have been protected since 2001, and that protection was through the Marine Living Resources Act, so the protection has always been there, and South Africa was one of the first countries to actually protect the species of Great White Sharks. From our side, we will continue investigating and generating more knowledge in our Oceans and Coastal research team in finding answers to these issues
Link: In Kwa Zulu Natal it’s a fine balance between keeping tourism alive without killing all the sharks
Geremy “In an ideal world we would like to see a system where we can keep humans and sharks apart and we have believed for a number of years that using electric fields is the best way to do that, and we have been looking now for 2 or 3 decades
Script: But they still haven’t found a workable solution the sea is an unrelenting force and developing a viable electric barrier is expensive
Link: There have been about 20 shark attacks in the last 15 years in Cape Waters and we have been doing shark barrier stories for the last two decades now they are developing something called a shark safe barrier.
Script: Taking their lead from seals which hide in kelp when hunted by sharks, Mike, Sara and American scientist Dr Craig O’Connell have been developing a magnetic kelp barrier for the last 4 years.
Mike “When the animal comes to the shark within one meter he can feel it even if it is dark or the water is dirty that forms a magnetic curtain as well
Mike ”Well we put the chum inside the barrier so the animals are highly motivated and so far we have not had one animal enter the barrier”
Derek Well I hope you keep that 100% record personally
Mike: “Ha ha well me to
Script: This barrier may work in Cape Waters but the Sharks board say it’s not a viable option for them
Geremy: The problem is that in KZN it’s a very open coastline so there is a huge challenge to maintain any sort of physical structure in the vicinity of the surf zone
Script: And the debate continues to rage on all fronts - be it barriers or numbers
Sara” My biggest concern is that while we are busy arguing about peer reviewed results, the animals are the ones that are suffering”

Mike “When the animal comes to the shark within one meter he can feel it even if it is dark or the water is dirty that forms a magnetic curtain as well Mike ”Well we put the chum inside the barrier so the animals are highly motivated and so far we have not had one animal enter the barrier” Derek Well I hope you keep that 100% record personally Mike: “Ha ha well me to Script: This barrier may work in Cape Waters but the Sharks board say it’s not a viable option for them Geremy: The problem is that in KZN it’s a very open coastline so there is a huge challenge to maintain any sort of physical structure in the vicinity of the surf zone Script: And the debate continues to rage on all fronts - be it barriers or numbers Sara” My biggest concern is that while we are busy arguing about peer reviewed results, the animals are the ones that are suffering” Invoicing Back references from Insert ID in Invoice: Title Author Last Updated Invoice for Extinction of the Great White Shark (4835 ) lizfish@iafrica.com 06 August 2016

metadata.Summary: The Great White Shark population along the South African coastline is facing extinction- there are insufficient breeding pairs to create genetic diversity, there is also only one species of Great Whites off our coastline. A six year study by Dr Sara Andreotti from the University of Stellenbosch along with “shark man” Michael Rutzen a shark behaviourist has found that there are between 353 to 522 Great Whites left and only 333 individuals can contribute offspring to the next population and can carry on the 14 million year lineage.
metadata.Further information: Dr Andreotti’s first study which Carte Blanche covered revealed that a sharks dorsal fin is like it’s thumb print. Andreotti has built a data base of photographs and has crossed checked it with the DNA samples collected from every shark they have photographed. Spending 4 years collecting samples and photographs, often at sea for two months at a time, with over 5000 siting’s, the data revealed an alarming situation. They were seeing the same sharks. They were migrating between Gansbaai, False Bay and Port Elizabeth but it was the same population, and there are only between 353 and 522. This study has confirmed what conservationists have feared, but now they have concrete evidence. Great Whites are supposedly a protected species yet The Natal Sharks Board is killing between 11 - 60 great whites annually, a staggering 10-15% of the population. South Africa also issues permits to legally long line sharks and so it is little wonder that the species is in such a dire state. Other reasons for the decline include baiting, poaching for the honour of owning a shark jaw; habitat encroachment and depletion of their food sources. The loss of an apex animal impacts the food chain, fewer sharks means more seals which in turn means fish stocks decline, coupled with over fishing food security for local fishermen is impacted
